nodes.name: Independence
nodes.text: Your party sets out from Missouri. You are following one of several emigrant routes west.

nodes.name: Elm Grove
nodes.text: A gathering place along the emigrant road. Check your supplies before moving toward the Wakarusa.

nodes.name: Wakarusa Creek
nodes.text: Wooded banks and limestone ledges make the Wakarusa a difficult approach. Travelers must judge the descent as well as the water before committing wagons and livestock.

nodes.name: Kansas River
nodes.text: The Kaw is a major crossing. French-Creole Pappin families and their Kanza relatives helped establish the ferry here. A documented period fare was $1 per wagon.

nodes.name: Big Vermilion
nodes.text: The road crosses Turkey Creek and the Little Vermilion to the Big Vermilion, a wooded creek with steep clay banks. Palmer's table counts intermediate camps along it; there is wood, water and grass here before the Big Blue.

nodes.name: Big Blue River
nodes.text: The Big Blue interrupts the emigrant road. No ferryman offers passage at your crossing. Judge the water before committing the wagon and livestock.

nodes.name: Little Blue River
nodes.text: The St. Joseph road joins from the east, and the trail strikes the Little Blue (Palmer's Republican fork of the Blue) near the Big Sandy. Days of good camps follow up the river's timbered bottom before the road climbs over to the Platte.

nodes.name: Platte River corridor
nodes.text: The broad Platte spreads into sandy channels. This river corridor is a long road west, not the end of the journey.

next.allocation_note: Authored subdivision of a period-guide aggregate; not a separately surveyed distance.

nodes.name: Fort Kearny site
nodes.text: Open ground on the south bank marks the new army post site. In 1848 construction began in June: expect tents, sod and adobe work, not a stockaded fortress or guaranteed supplies.

next.allocation_note: Authored subdivision of a period-guide aggregate; not a separately surveyed distance.

nodes.name: South Platte crossing
nodes.text: The sandy South Platte interrupts the westward road. Channels and quicksand make depth alone a poor guide. There is no later bridge here.

nodes.name: Ash Hollow
nodes.text: A steep descent leads into a sheltered hollow. Water and vegetation offer relief after exposed prairie. Lower wagons carefully rather than rushing the slope.

nodes.name: Courthouse and Jail Rocks
nodes.text: Large pale rock formations rise from the plains. Palmer called one the Solitary Tower; later travelers used the Courthouse and Jail names.

nodes.name: Chimney Rock
nodes.text: A narrow spire rises above an eroded mound. Travelers recognize this landmark from guidebooks, but the mountain crossings still lie ahead.

nodes.name: Scotts Bluff / Robidoux route
nodes.text: The bluffs block a direct road along the river. In 1848 wagons swing south toward Robidoux Pass; the later Mitchell Pass road is not open.

nodes.name: Fort John / Laramie
nodes.text: An adobe-walled private trading post stands on the Laramie. It is still Fort John in 1848; the army purchase and the familiar military buildings come later.
nodes.advice: Check food for the next long leg, allow for days lost to weather, and keep money for later supplies. A post is a chance to prepare, not a guarantee that the journey ahead is safe.

nodes.name: Horse Shoe Creek
nodes.text: Past the Big Spring and Bitter Cottonwood, the road over the Black Hills reaches Horse Shoe Creek, a clear stream with timber and grass. The hills ahead are rough on wheels and feet.

nodes.name: Deer Creek
nodes.text: The road returns to the Platte at Deer Creek, a favorite camp with good grass, cottonwood and fish. Many companies rest here before the crossing of the North Fork.

nodes.name: North Platte crossing
nodes.text: The trail returns to the North Platte. A crossing commits livestock and loaded wagons to the current. Wait for better water if the stage is unfavorable.

nodes.name: Willow Spring
nodes.text: After the Mineral Springs, where the water is bad and cattle sicken, Willow Spring is a welcome good camp: cold water, willows for fuel and some grass, a long day short of the Sweetwater.

nodes.name: Independence Rock
nodes.text: A broad rounded granite outcrop stands beside the Sweetwater. Earlier travelers left names here. Reaching it by early July was a useful seasonal ambition, not a magical deadline.

nodes.name: Devil's Gate
nodes.text: The Sweetwater cuts a narrow gap through dark rock. Wagons go around the obstruction; the river gorge is not the wagon road.

snow_country.note: Authored winter risk, not reconstructed 1848 weather. Late parties met snow in the high country: Barlow's 1845 party on Mount Hood, the 1846 Applegate and Donner parties, the 1856 handcart companies near South Pass. Snow blocks the road some days; with no grass, animals lose condition even in camp and worn-out animals can die.

nodes.name: South Pass
nodes.text: The Continental Divide is a broad, gently rising saddle here, rather than a narrow alpine notch. Your wagon can cross, but distance, weather and worn livestock still matter.
nodes.advice: Past Pacific Spring the road forks. The southern road goes by Bridger's post; Greenwood's northern cutoff is shorter but crosses forty miles without water. Shorter did not mean easier.

nodes.name: Little Sandy / parting of the roads
nodes.text: Beyond Pacific Spring the road forks. Palmer's southern road runs by Bridger's trading post to Bear River. Greenwood's northern cutoff strikes the Green River about forty miles upstream and saves two and a half days of driving, but forty of its miles have no water and little grass.

next.label: Take the southern road toward Green River crossing and Fort Bridger
Take Greenwood's Cutoff Â· 46 miles to the Green, 40 without water

nodes.name: Green River / Greenwood's Cutoff
nodes.text: After the long dry drive from the Big Sandy, the cutoff strikes the Green River about forty miles above the southern crossing. Animals smell the water before you see it. The current here is swift and cold.

nodes.name: Green River crossing
nodes.text: You reach the Green River on Palmer's southern route, downstream of the crossing used by Greenwood's Cutoff. Mountain men and Mormon ferrymen take wagons over for pay; the fare doubles in high water.

nodes.name: Fort Bridger
nodes.text: Bridger and Vasquez trade along Black's Fork. Their log-and-earth trading establishment is not the army fort that develops in the late 1850s.

next.label: Take the Mormon road to Great Salt Lake City · about 121 miles
next.allocation_note: William Clayton, The Latter-Day Saints' Emigrants' Guide (1848): Fort Bridger to the City of the Great Salt Lake about 121 1/2 miles, by Echo Canyon and Emigration Canyon.

nodes.advice: Check food for the next long leg, allow for days lost to weather, and keep money for later supplies. A post is a chance to prepare, not a guarantee that the journey ahead is safe.

nodes.name: Bear River valley
nodes.text: The road from Bridger's post comes down to the Bear River, where Greenwood's northern cutoff rejoins it near Smith's Fork. The valley has grass, willows and good water; Big Hill and the Bear River narrows lie ahead.

nodes.name: Great Salt Lake City
nodes.text: The Latter-day Saints reached this valley in July 1847 and have laid out a city of wide streets around the Old Fort. In 1848 crickets and frost cut the harvest; food is scarce and dear, but the settlers want cloth, tools and cattle. North, Hensley's new cutoff runs past the Bear River to the California road and on to the Raft River.

next.label: Take Hensley's Salt Lake cutoff north to the Raft River · about 230 miles
next.allocation_note: Authored estimate: about 180 miles from the city north of the lake to the California road near the City of Rocks (Salt Lake Cutoff, opened by Samuel Hensley's pack train in summer 1848 and made a wagon road by returning Mormon Battalion men in September 1848), then about 50 miles down the Raft River valley to the Oregon road.

nodes.name: Soda Springs
nodes.text: Mineral water bubbles among pale deposits in the Bear River country. Travelers describe the unusual pools and crusted formations around this familiar stopping place.

nodes.name: Fort Hall
nodes.text: The Hudson's Bay Company post offers a place to seek supplies and information. Palmer's earlier guide quotes emergency flour at twenty dollars per hundred pounds, but availability is not assured by a price.
nodes.advice: Check food for the next long leg, allow for days lost to weather, and keep money for later supplies. A post is a chance to prepare, not a guarantee that the journey ahead is safe.

nodes.name: American Falls
nodes.text: Past the crossing of the Portneuf, the Snake drops over a broad ledge of dark rock. Shoshone and Bannock families fish below the falls in season.

nodes.name: Raft River
nodes.text: At Cassia Creek and the Raft River the California road turns off south toward the City of Rocks. Oregon companies keep west along the Snake into dry sage country.

nodes.name: Salmon Falls
nodes.text: Shoshone fishermen spear and trap salmon at the falls and dry them on racks. Emigrants trade powder, clothing or fishhooks for fish. The road beyond climbs to the first crossing of the Snake.

nodes.name: Snake River / Three Island area
nodes.text: Palmer's first crossing of Lewis's River lies in the Snake corridor. The Three Island area offered an emigrant crossing, but deep channels made it dangerous.

nodes.name: Fort Boise / Snake crossing
nodes.text: The Hudson's Bay Company adobe post stands near the Boise and Snake confluence, far from the later military Fort Boise. After visiting, the guide's route crosses the Snake again before turning toward the Malheur.
nodes.advice: This is the old Hudson's Bay Company post near the river confluence, not the United States Army post built near modern Boise in 1863.

nodes.name: Malheur River
nodes.text: Across the Snake from the post, the road reaches the Malheur, where hot springs steam beside the cold stream. Ahead the trail leaves the Snake for good at the bend and climbs to Burnt River.

nodes.name: Burnt River
nodes.text: The route leaves the Snake country and follows the broken Burnt River corridor. Steep ground and limited grazing strain teams that were comfortable on the Platte.

nodes.name: Powder River valley
nodes.text: After the rough Burnt River road, the Powder valley opens ahead. Palmer's lone pine is already described as a stump: this illustration does not invent a living landmark tree.

nodes.name: Grande Ronde valley
nodes.text: A broad valley offers grass before the Blue Mountains. Resting here uses provisions, but a worn team faces a difficult climb if you hurry onward.

snow_country.note: Authored winter risk, not reconstructed 1848 weather. Late parties met snow in the high country: Barlow's 1845 party on Mount Hood, the 1846 Applegate and Donner parties, the 1856 handcart companies near South Pass. Snow blocks the road some days; with no grass, animals lose condition even in camp and worn-out animals can die.

nodes.name: Blue Mountains
nodes.text: Forested ridges replace the open river valleys. The ascent and descent demand care with loads and animals. The main road descends to the Umatilla; an older road turns north to the Hudson's Bay Company's Fort Walla Walla, through country at war since the killings at the Whitman mission last November.

next.label: Descend to the Umatilla on the main road
Detour to Fort Walla Walla Â· Cayuse War country, about 20 miles longer
next.allocation_note: Authored estimate: about 30 miles from the Blue Mountains to the Waiilatpu mission site and about 25 from Waiilatpu to the Hudson's Bay post. Not a Palmer table row.

nodes.name: Fort Walla Walla
nodes.text: The Hudson's Bay Company's Fort Nez PercÃ©s stands where the Walla Walla River meets the Columbia. Since the killings at Waiilatpu the post has been a place of ransom and refuge; most emigrants this year avoid it. Supplies are scarce and dear.

next.allocation_note: Authored estimate of about 25 miles down the Columbia's south bank to the Umatilla's mouth. Not a Palmer table row.

nodes.advice: The road down the south bank of the Columbia rejoins the main trail at the John Day. Volunteers and Cayuse bands are both abroad; travel watchfully.

nodes.name: Umatilla River
nodes.text: The descent reaches the Umatilla country, home to Indigenous communities long before wagon migration. The road approaches the Columbia through dry rolling hills.

nodes.name: Columbia River at the Umatilla
nodes.text: The Umatilla meets the Columbia in sand and sage. The road from Fort Walla Walla along the south bank joins the main road here, and both follow the great river west toward the John Day.

nodes.name: John Day River
nodes.text: The river cuts a dry canyon on the way to the Columbia. Water at a crossing does not mean that grass and easy travel are abundant on the next stretch.

nodes.name: Deschutes River
nodes.text: Palmer's Falls River is the Deschutes. Its channel and current make this another serious obstacle before The Dalles.

nodes.name: The Dalles
nodes.text: The Columbia narrows among exposed rock and rapids. Here the overland road ends for many: the Barlow wagon road climbs south of Mount Hood, while others build rafts or hire boats and take their chances on the river.

next.allocation_note: Authored subdivision of a period-guide aggregate; not a separately surveyed distance.
next.label: Take the Barlow road south of Mount Hood
Build a raft and float the Columbia Â· 3 days building
next.allocation_note: NPS Columbia Gorge narrative: the river flowed smoothly for about forty miles below The Dalles to the Cascades. Not a Palmer table row.

nodes.advice: The river route used rafts, boats and portages, with livestock driven along trails. A raft was not an uninterrupted ride: wind pins boats to the shore and the Cascades must be portaged or run. The Barlow road is longer, costs a toll and ends at Laurel Hill.

nodes.name: Cascades of the Columbia

river_winter.note: Authored. Late parties took the river to avoid Barlow snow (NPS, Overlanders in the Columbia River Gorge, 1840-1870: the reach from The Dalles was usually windy). The lower Columbia froze in hard winters: at Vancouver on January 26, 1847 the ice held HMS Modeste (Clark County history). On winter river days the cold costs everyone chill_damage health and wind pins the raft ashore by windbound_chance; in a hard winter (hard_winter_chance per winter) no raft launches in frozen_months and a raft already afloat is pinned by running ice at ice_bound_chance. A wreck in icy water drowns wreck_drowning_factor times as often.

nodes.text: The river that carried your raft from The Dalles breaks white over the Cascades, about six miles of rapids. Parties unload and carry their goods around on a rough portage path, often with Chinookan or Hudson's Bay Company help, or gamble on running the water.

next.allocation_note: Six miles of rapids (NPS) plus authored modern river-mile estimates: about 44 from the lower Cascades to the Willamette's mouth and about 26 up the Willamette to the falls at Oregon City.

snow_country.note: Authored winter risk, not reconstructed 1848 weather. Late parties met snow in the high country: Barlow's 1845 party on Mount Hood, the 1846 Applegate and Donner parties, the 1856 handcart companies near South Pass. Snow blocks the road some days; with no grass, animals lose condition even in camp and worn-out animals can die.

nodes.name: Barlow Road / Mount Hood
nodes.text: The toll road opened in 1846. It climbs through the forests south of Mount Hood. The charter rate was five dollars per wagon and ten cents per head of livestock; paying does not make the road easy.

next.allocation_note: Authored subdivision of a period-guide aggregate; not a separately surveyed distance.

nodes.closure_note: Authored season. Barlow Pass stands above 4,000 feet south of Mount Hood. Barlow's own 1845 party was caught by autumn snow and cached its wagons at Fort Deposit; in 1849 a military train abandoned 45 wagons on the road after its mules starved. Wagons are shut out November through April; walkers and pack trains may still go around.

nodes.name: Laurel Hill
nodes.text: The descent is steep enough to require ropes and carefully controlled wagons. Lightening a load and taking time are practical alternatives to a hurried descent.

next.allocation_note: Authored subdivision of a period-guide aggregate; not a separately surveyed distance.

nodes.name: Eagle Creek / Foster country
nodes.text: The road descends toward the Willamette settlements. You still need provisions and care for the team; reaching the forest's western edge is not arrival in Oregon City.

next.allocation_note: Authored subdivision of a period-guide aggregate; not a separately surveyed distance.

nodes.name: Oregon City / Willamette Falls
nodes.text: You have reached Oregon City beside Willamette Falls. The overland journey is complete. Surviving the trail is an ending, not a promise of an effortless new life.

distance_note: 1938 reported guide miles. Kearny position and four Barlow sublegs are authored allocations within period aggregate distances; not surveyed coordinates.
